newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to inject funds to beat crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to inject funds to beat crisis.

text.p: Bangladeshi officials and bankers said on Friday they hoped a government decision to inject $368 million into commercial banks would be enough to overcome fears of a banking collapse.
Finance Ministry secretary Syed Amirul Mulk said the government would provide commercial banks with funds to help them weather a liquidity crisis that could have forced some to shut down.
But one central bank official said the government might still have to close two banks.
"Two of them in the private sector are in severe crisis and may have to be shut down," said the official, who did not want to be named.

Mulk said the central bank had identified seven of the country's 32 banks that were in bad shape due to the liquidity crisis, but he declined to name them for fear of creating alarm among depositors. Ten of the 32 banks are foreign owned.
"I don't think the country's banking system will collapse due to the liquidity crisis. The government is taking all steps to overcome the weakness of the sector," he told Reuters.
Central Bank Governor Lutfar Rahman Sarkar triggered the alarm on Tuesday when he said that the "country's banking system is now on the verge of collapse."

Sarkar estimated the amount of outstanding bank loans at 130 billion taka and said the country did not have adequate laws to deal with defaulters. "The defaulters are taking the advantage of legal loopholes."
Central bank officials said on Friday the government would provide 16 billion taka ($368 million) to fund-starved banks to improve their liquidity position.
The bank crisis has hit the stock market as well, with the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) benchmark index dropping 9.56 percent in the three days to Thursday amid signs of panic selling among investors.
Banks and the stock exchange were all closed for the Moslem weekend on Friday, but are due to open as normal on Saturday.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank had asked the government to close the worst hit banks, officials said, but they added that five institutions had improved their position following warnings from the central bank.

Ibrahim Khaled, managing director of Bangladesh's largest state-owned institution, Sonali Bank, told Reuters Financial Television that 40 percent of private commercial bank loans were regarded as bad debt, while the figure for state-owned banks was 30 percent.
He said politically dictated loans during the 1980s had been a major cause of the bad debt problem.
But he called the present position of the banks "generally not bad" and questioned whether Sarkar had ever issued such a stark warning.
Khaled said he believed the State Bank chief had been misquoted in a central bank press release, although Sarker has not issued any correction.
Khaled acknowledged two banks in the private sector were causing concern but said all other banks, including those in the state sector, were showing "acceptable results."
Commercial bankers said as a result of the liquidity scare, they had started reining back on lending.
"We are now very cautious in lending. We are offering loans to only new small borrowers at the moment," said one official with the Sonali bank. ($1=43.65 rupee)
